title: Sales Leadership Communication
subtitle: The internal language of sales leadership — coaching conversations, pipeline reviews, target-setting, and the strategic communication that drives team performance
description: Sales leadership requires a distinct set of communication skills that are entirely different from those used in customer-facing conversations. Where a salesperson persuades, a sales leader coaches. Where a salesperson closes, a sales leader develops capability. The most effective sales managers spend the majority of their time in conversations that build their team's judgement rather than providing answers — asking questions that help a rep discover the right course of action rather than prescribing it. This lesson teaches the internal language of B2B sales leadership: how to run a pipeline review that surfaces real risk rather than polished projections, how to coach without telling, how to set and communicate targets in a way that creates clarity rather than anxiety, and how to communicate strategic direction in a way that enables every member of the team to execute with autonomy.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley, now a sales manager, runs a pipeline review with Jordan — a rep whose enterprise deal has been stuck for three weeks; she coaches Jordan through the deal using questions rather than instructions, and then aligns on a forecasting commitment and next steps

vocabulary.definition: The revenue target assigned to a salesperson or team for a defined period — typically a quarter or a financial year. Quota is the foundational metric of individual sales performance: a rep at 100% of quota has closed exactly their assigned target; a rep at 120% has over-delivered. Quota-setting involves balancing historical performance, market opportunity, and organisational growth targets.
vocabulary.example: Riley said to Jordan: Your quota for Q3 is £320,000 — that's a 15% increase on Q2 attainment, which reflects both the growth in your territory and the maturity of your pipeline. I want to be transparent about how we got to that number: £200,000 represents the baseline expectation from accounts in your territory, and the remaining £120,000 represents your stretch — three new logos at average deal size.

vocabulary.definition: The percentage of quota achieved by a salesperson or team in a given period — the primary metric of sales performance. A rep at 120% attainment has closed 120% of their assigned quota. Attainment is typically reviewed at quarter-end, but tracking in-period attainment allows managers and reps to identify risk and adjust behaviour before the quarter closes.
vocabulary.example: Riley reviewed the team's performance: Jordan, at the midpoint of Q3, your attainment is 58% of quota. That sounds below target, but the pipeline coverage is 3.8x — which means if the top four deals close as expected, you'll land at around 115%. The risk I want to explore is that three of those four deals have been in the pipeline for more than 60 days without a clear next step. That's what we need to address today.

vocabulary.definition: In sales leadership, the ongoing process of developing a rep's judgement, skills, and self-awareness through questioning, observation, and structured reflection — rather than through instruction or direction. The most effective coaching conversations ask questions that help the rep discover the right answer rather than providing the answer directly, building capability that transfers to future situations.
vocabulary.example: Riley's coaching philosophy was explicit: My job in pipeline reviews is not to tell you what to do. It's to help you think better about what you're doing. Every question I ask is designed to surface something you already know but haven't yet applied. If I tell you to call the champion by Thursday, you'll call the champion by Thursday. If I help you understand why calling the champion by Thursday matters, you'll start making that decision yourself.

vocabulary.definition: The ratio of the total value of deals in a rep's pipeline to their quota — a key health metric for predicting whether a rep will make their number. A pipeline coverage of 3x means the rep has three times their quota in active opportunities. Healthy coverage ratios vary by industry and deal complexity, but 3x to 4x is a common standard in B2B enterprise sales.
vocabulary.example: Riley explained the coverage concern: Jordan's headline coverage is 3.8x — which looks healthy. But when I strip out the three deals that have been stuck for more than 60 days without a defined next step, effective coverage drops to 2.1x. That's below the threshold for confidence at this stage of the quarter. We need to either unstick those deals or replace them with qualified pipeline before mid-quarter.

vocabulary.definition: A prediction of the revenue expected to close in a given period — typically categorised by confidence level: commit (deals the rep is certain will close), best case (deals that could close with a positive outcome), and upside (stretch deals that are possible but not expected). Forecasting accuracy is a critical skill for sales leaders, whose own commitments to senior leadership are based on aggregating their team's forecasts.
vocabulary.example: Riley asked Jordan: What are you committing to the forecast this quarter? Not best case — what is your commit number? The number you'd stake your credibility on, that you'd be confident telling me will close regardless of how the next eight weeks play out. I need that number to be accurate, because my commit to the VP is the sum of eight forecasts, and one that's 40% wrong at the rep level creates a problem at the leadership level.

vocabulary.definition: Any factor that makes a specific deal less likely to close on time or at the expected value — including missing stakeholders, an absent champion, no agreed next step, a competitor gaining ground, or a change in the buyer's internal priorities. In a pipeline review, surfacing deal risk is the primary analytical task: the manager is looking for the difference between what the rep says and what the deal's actual behaviour suggests.
vocabulary.example: Riley named the deal risk directly: Jordan, the deal has been in 'negotiation' stage for 47 days. The last logged activity was a call three weeks ago with no recorded next step. In my experience, that's not a deal that's progressing quietly — that's a deal that's stalling. The question is whether the stall is visible and being managed, or whether it's a slow fade that neither party has explicitly acknowledged yet.

vocabulary.definition: The period of time it takes a new salesperson to reach full quota productivity after joining a team — typically three to six months in B2B sales depending on the deal complexity and the rep's prior experience. Ramp plans define the expected attainment trajectory during this period: a new rep might be expected to reach 25% of quota in month two, 50% in month three, and 75% by month five.
vocabulary.example: Riley introduced the new rep to the team: Alex is in month two of their ramp — which means we're expecting approximately 30% of quota attainment this quarter, not 100%. That's not underperformance; it's the plan. My job during ramp is to maximise the quality of the learning, not the quantity of the deals. By the end of month four, I want Alex to be running deals independently with confidence — and that takes time to build correctly.

vocabulary.definition: The percentage of qualified sales opportunities that convert to closed business — a key metric for evaluating pipeline quality, competitive positioning, and process effectiveness. Win rate is typically calculated on qualified opportunities (excluding deals lost at the qualification stage) and tracked by segment, territory, and rep to identify patterns in where deals are being won and lost.
vocabulary.example: Riley reflected on Jordan's win rate trend: Your win rate on enterprise deals above £200,000 has dropped from 38% to 24% over the past two quarters. That's a significant shift — and the question is whether it reflects a change in the competitive landscape, a shift in the quality of opportunities being qualified, a change in your approach at the late stage, or something about how you're handling objections. I don't know which one it is — but you might. What do you think is behind it?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: Walk me through where this deal is — not the pitch, tell me where the deal actually is
phrasalVerbs.definition: The standard opening of a coaching pipeline review — distinguishing between a rep's optimistic narrative about a deal (the pitch) and the objective status of the deal based on observable facts (last activity, agreed next step, stakeholder engagement). This distinction signals to the rep that the manager is looking for honest analysis, not a sales story.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley opened the pipeline review with Jordan: Walk me through where the Meridian deal is — not the pitch version, tell me where it actually is. What was the last meaningful interaction? What was agreed as the next step? Who have you spoken to in the last two weeks — and who have you not spoken to that you should have?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: What's your plan to close this before quarter end?
phrasalVerbs.definition: The coaching question for surfacing whether a rep has a concrete, executable close plan — or whether their forecast is based on hope rather than strategy. A rep who can answer this question specifically (named actions, named stakeholders, specific dates) has a real plan. A rep who answers vaguely ('we're in conversations') does not.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley asked: You've told me this deal is in negotiate stage and likely to close this quarter. What's your plan to close it before quarter end? Not the general intention — the specific sequence of events: what happens next, who is involved, what decision has to be made by whom, and by what date. Walk me through the close plan step by step.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: What would you do differently if you could go back to the first call?
phrasalVerbs.definition: The reflective coaching question for helping a rep identify what they would change about their approach — without the manager prescribing the answer. It invites self-critique and pattern recognition, which builds transferable learning rather than one-off advice.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley asked Jordan: The deal has been stuck for 47 days. Looking back — what would you do differently if you could go back to the first call with Meridian? I'm not looking for the 'right' answer, I'm curious what you think. Because whatever comes out of that reflection is probably the most useful thing to take into the next deal you open.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: I'm going to commit [X] to the forecast — what are you committing?
phrasalVerbs.definition: The question for driving forecast discipline — asking the rep to name a number they will stand behind with full confidence, rather than offering a range or a best-case figure. The manager's own commitment creates a shared accountability structure: both the rep and the manager are putting their credibility on the line.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley said: I'm going to commit £280,000 from the team to the forecast for this week's leadership review. That means I need your commit number — not your best case, not the optimistic version. The number that you are certain about, that you would be comfortable having reviewed at the end of the quarter against actuals. What are you committing from your pipeline?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: The strategy for Q3 is [X] — every rep should be able to explain their personal version in 60 seconds
phrasalVerbs.definition: The phrase for communicating strategic direction in a way that requires active translation — not passive listening. Asking each rep to explain their personal version forces them to connect the strategy to their specific territory, accounts, and activities, which reveals both understanding and gaps.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley briefed the team: The strategy for Q3 is enterprise expansion — deepening relationships in our top 20 accounts rather than chasing net new logos. Every rep on this team should be able to explain their personal version of that strategy in 60 seconds: which three or four of your accounts represent the expansion opportunity, what the specific growth lever is in each, and what you're doing differently this quarter to activate it.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: I want to hear your thinking — tell me what you see and what you'd do
phrasalVerbs.definition: The coaching invitation for creating space for the rep to lead the analysis — signalling that the manager's role in this conversation is to listen and respond, not to direct. It positions the rep as the agent of the analysis and the manager as the thinking partner.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley said to Jordan: Before I share any observations, I want to hear your thinking. Tell me what you see when you look at this deal — what's working, what's not, and what you'd do next if I weren't in the room. I'll ask questions after. The point is not for me to give you the answer — it's for you to work through the analysis out loud so we can both see where the gaps are.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Jordan, let's start with the Meridian deal. Walk me through where it actually is — not the pitch version. Last activity, last agreed next step, and who you've spoken to in the past two weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: The deal is in negotiate stage. We had a strong call three weeks ago — Marcus was engaged, the numbers worked. I've been waiting for him to come back with feedback on the proposal.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Three weeks with no contact and no agreed next step is the first thing I want to focus on. What was the explicit next step at the end of that call?

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: We said we'd... be in touch when they'd had a chance to review internally.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: 'Be in touch' is not a next step — it's the absence of one. I'm not saying that to criticise the call; I'm saying it because that's where the [[deal risk:any factor making a specific deal less likely to close on time — including missing stakeholders, no agreed next step, or a silent prospect]] is sitting. A deal that's left to drift is rarely a deal that comes back on its own. What's your read on why Marcus has gone quiet?

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: Honestly — I'm not sure. It could be internal process. It could be that something has changed and he doesn't want to be the one to say it.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Those are two very different situations. One of them is manageable; the other may mean the deal is lost. I want to hear your thinking — tell me what you see and what you'd do if you were going to call Marcus today.

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: I'd call to check in. See if there's anything I can help with on the internal side.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That's a reasonable instinct — but 'check in' is still vague. What's the specific purpose of the call — and what would a successful outcome look like? A good reengagement call has a reason for calling beyond 'I haven't heard from you', a specific piece of [[decision support:materials or information that help the buyer make the internal case]] to offer, and a named next step to close on. What would your version of that look like for Meridian?

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: I could call saying I've prepared a CFO-ready one-pager — ask if that would be useful. And close on a specific date to reconnect.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That's the call. Now — what would you do differently if you could go back to the first call? Not to beat yourself up — because if we can identify the pattern, the learning applies to every deal in your pipeline.

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: I'd have closed on a more specific next step at every meeting. And I'd have identified the internal champion earlier rather than relying only on Marcus.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Both of those are the right diagnosis — and I want to make sure they go into your [[coaching:the ongoing development of a rep's judgement through questioning and reflection rather than instruction]] log so we can revisit them. Now — let's talk [[forecast:a prediction of revenue expected to close in a given period, categorised by confidence level: commit, best case, upside]]. Your [[pipeline coverage:the ratio of total pipeline value to quota — healthy is typically 3x to 4x]] is 3.8x on paper, but if I strip the three deals that have been stuck for more than 60 days, effective coverage drops to 2.1x. What are you committing to the forecast this quarter?

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: My best case is £280,000 — but my commit is probably closer to £190,000.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I'm going to commit £190,000 from your pipeline to the leadership forecast — which means your [[quota:the revenue target assigned to a rep for a defined period — the foundational metric of individual performance]] for the quarter is going to require you to either unstick two of those three deals or add qualified pipeline before week six. What's your plan to get there?

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: I have two deals in late qualification that I've been holding back from the forecast. If either converts to proposal stage this week, the coverage picture looks very different.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Then let's put those in the plan explicitly. The Q3 strategy is enterprise expansion — not net new volume. So every deal you're working should map to that frame. Call Marcus today with the CFO one-pager, log the call, and close on a specific date for the next interaction. And bring those two qualification deals to Thursday's review so I can see what's actually there.

questions: Think about the best manager or coach you've ever worked with — in sales, sport, or any professional context. What made their feedback effective? What did they do differently from managers who gave advice that didn't help?

In your experience, what is the difference between a manager who tells their team what to do and one who coaches them to figure it out themselves? Which approach produces better results in the long run — and why?

Imagine you are running a review of your team's pipeline. One of your reps has a deal that's been stuck for a month. What questions would you ask them — and how would you balance honest challenge with supportive development?

completeSentenceExercise.instructions: Choose the correct word or phrase to complete each sentence. Only one answer is correct.

items.sentence: Jordan's win rate on enterprise deals _____ significantly over the past two quarters — from 38% to 24% — which suggests a pattern worth investigating before it becomes structural.
options: has raised
has risen
has been raised
items.explanation: 'Has risen' is correct — 'rise' is an intransitive verb (it does not take a direct object). 'The win rate has risen' means the win rate went up by itself. 'Raise' is a transitive verb that requires a direct object — someone or something raises something else: 'we raised the quota', 'the manager raised the target'. 'Has raised' would need an object: 'Jordan has raised the win rate' (someone actively raised it). 'Has been raised' is passive — it implies someone raised it externally. Since win rate changes on its own (no agent is raising it), the correct intransitive verb is 'rise': 'the rate has risen', 'revenue has risen', 'attainment has risen'. The pair to remember: raise (transitive) / rise (intransitive) — the same distinction as lay/lie.

items.sentence: In the pipeline review, Riley avoided _____ the outcome — she asked questions designed to help Jordan reach the conclusion independently.
options: to discuss about
discussing
to discuss
items.explanation: 'Discussing' (gerund) is correct — 'avoid' is always followed by a gerund, never by a 'to' infinitive. 'Avoid discussing', 'avoid prescribing', 'avoid telling' — not 'avoid to discuss'. In addition, 'discuss' is transitive and does not take the preposition 'about' — 'discuss the outcome', not 'discuss about the outcome'. 'Discuss about' is a very common error in formal writing, but 'discuss' already carries the meaning of 'talk about', so adding 'about' is redundant. The correct forms: 'avoid discussing the outcome' (gerund, no 'about') — neither 'avoid to discuss' (infinitive is wrong after 'avoid') nor 'avoid discussing about' (preposition is wrong after 'discuss').

items.sentence: Riley told Jordan to _____ a specific close plan rather than a general intention to 'stay in touch'.
options: focus on to develop
focus on developing
focus to develop
items.explanation: 'Focus on developing' is correct — 'focus on' is a phrasal verb that takes a gerund as its complement, not an infinitive. 'Focus on + gerund': 'focus on developing the plan', 'focus on closing the deal', 'focus on building the relationship'. 'Focus on to develop' is a hybrid error: 'on' requires a gerund, not 'to' + infinitive. 'Focus to develop' (without 'on') is non-standard — 'focus' as a verb typically requires 'on' when it takes a complement: 'focus on X'. Compare with other phrasal verbs that take gerunds: 'insist on signing', 'succeed in closing', 'concentrate on developing'. The pattern: preposition + gerund, never preposition + 'to' + infinitive.

items.sentence: Riley's _____ to the team was consistent: ask more questions, prescribe fewer answers, and build capability rather than dependency.
options: advise
advice
advising
items.explanation: 'Advice' is the noun — 'Riley's advice to the team'. 'Advise' is the verb — 'Riley advised the team'. These two forms are frequently confused, particularly in written English, where the spelling difference ('c' vs 's') is the only distinction. The noun: 'advice' (uncountable — 'a piece of advice', not 'an advice'). The verb: 'advise' — 'she advised them to focus on questions'. 'Advising' is the present participle of the verb, which cannot be used as the subject complement here ('Riley's advising' would need a different sentence structure). The rule: advice (noun, uncountable, ends in -ce) / advise (verb, ends in -se) — the same pattern as practice/practise, licence/license in British English.

items.sentence: The effective coverage — _____ deals stuck for more than 60 days are removed — drops to 2.1x, which is below the threshold for forecasting confidence at this stage of the quarter.
options: after
once
when
items.explanation: 'Once' is the most precise choice here — 'once those deals are removed' means 'after the action of removing them has been completed'. It implies a single, complete action with a clear before-and-after state. 'After' is also grammatically correct and nearly synonymous, but in formal analytical writing 'once' is the preferred choice when describing a condition that, when fulfilled, produces a specific result: 'once the adjustment is made', 'once risk is factored in', 'once the exclusions are applied'. 'When' is more general and can imply a recurring or habitual action, which is less precise for a one-time analytical adjustment. In conditional analytical statements — 'once X is done, Y follows' — 'once' is the most concise and formal choice.

items.sentence: A rep who cannot explain their personal version of the Q3 strategy in 60 seconds _____ understood it well enough to execute it.
options: hasn't
hasn't probably
probably hasn't
items.explanation: 'Probably hasn't' is correct — the adverb 'probably' should be placed between the auxiliary verb 'has' and the main verb 'understood', or immediately before the auxiliary in a negative construction: 'probably hasn't understood'. In formal English, adverbs of probability ('probably', 'certainly', 'possibly', 'clearly') are placed immediately before the main verb in positive sentences ('has probably understood') or between the first auxiliary and the main verb in negatives ('probably hasn't understood' / 'hasn't probably understood'). 'Hasn't probably understood' is awkward and non-standard because 'probably' is displaced too far from the verbal group. 'Hasn't' alone (without 'probably') would be correct but assertive — here 'probably' is needed because it is an inference, not a certainty.

chooseResponse.instructions: Read what the sales rep says in the pipeline review. Choose the best response from the three options.

items.customerLine: The deal is going well — I think it'll close this quarter. Marcus is engaged and the numbers work.
options: Great — I'll put it in the forecast at full value for Q3. Let me know if anything changes.

I want to test that. When was the last time you spoke to Marcus, what was agreed as the next step at the end of that conversation, and who else in his organisation have you spoken to in the past two weeks? I'm not questioning your read — I want to make sure the evidence supports the optimism.
I've seen a lot of deals like this stall at the last minute. Have you identified all the internal stakeholders who need to approve? That's usually where things go wrong.
items.explanation: Option B is the right response — it tests the optimism with specific, observable facts rather than accepting the narrative at face value. A good pipeline review manager distinguishes between a rep's confidence (which can be influenced by effort, relationship, and wishful thinking) and the deal's actual observable status (last contact, last next step, stakeholder breadth). Option A accepts the rep's assessment without scrutiny — which is exactly the behaviour that produces inaccurate forecasts. Option C is critical and challenging, but it leads with a concern ('I've seen a lot of deals like this stall') rather than with data-driven questions — which can feel like skepticism rather than coaching.

items.customerLine: I'm not sure what to do with this deal. It feels like it's drifting and I don't know why.
options: You need to call the buyer today and be direct about the status. Ask them whether they're still planning to move forward or not.

Before I tell you what I'd do — tell me what you see when you look at it honestly. What's working, what's not, and what's the one thing you've been avoiding doing that you probably know you should do?
Deals drift when there's no urgency. Have you tried applying a deadline — a price that's only valid until the end of the month, for instance?
items.explanation: Option B is the coaching response — it creates space for the rep to lead the analysis before the manager shares any perspective. 'What's the one thing you've been avoiding doing?' is a particularly effective coaching question because reps usually know the answer; they need permission to say it out loud. Option A gives a direct instruction ('call the buyer today') — which may be the right action but does not develop the rep's ability to diagnose and respond to drift in future deals. Option C prescribes a tactic (an artificial price deadline) before understanding the cause of the drift — which may be entirely the wrong approach if the deal is stuck for a different reason.

items.customerLine: My best case for the quarter is £300,000 — but I'm not sure I'd commit to all of it.
options: Let's go with £280,000 as a compromise — that gives you some room and still keeps us on track for the team target.

What I need from you is two numbers, not one. Tell me your commit — the number you'd stake your credibility on regardless of how the next eight weeks play out. And separately, tell me what would need to happen for you to land the full £300,000. Those are different conversations, and I need them both to forecast accurately.
Best case and commit are often closer than reps think — let's say £270,000 and manage from there.
items.explanation: Option B is the most effective response — it drives the disciplined distinction between commit and best case that is the foundation of accurate forecasting. By asking for two separate numbers and the conditions that would deliver the higher figure, the manager gets both an honest forecast and a useful action plan. Option A negotiates a 'compromise' figure — which is neither the rep's honest commit nor their best case, and therefore produces an inaccurate forecast. Option C sets a number without understanding the rep's reasoning — which gives the appearance of precision without the underlying intelligence that makes a forecast reliable.

spotTheMistake.instructions: Read the pipeline review conversation. Three lines have a mistake. Can you find them?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Walk me through where the Meridian deal is — not the pitch version, tell me where it actually stands based on observable facts.

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: We had a strong call three weeks ago. The deal has raised to negotiate stage and I'm waiting for Marcus to come back.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Three weeks with no contact is a deal risk signal. I'd like to discuss about your reengagement plan — what's the specific purpose of the call you'd make today?

dialogue.speaker: Jordan
dialogue.text: I'd call offering a CFO one-pager as decision support — and close on a specific next step rather than leaving it open.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That's the right structure. Now — what would you do differently if you could go back? I want you to focus on to identify the pattern, because that's what makes this conversation valuable for the next deal.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Good. Let's close on a commit number and a concrete action plan for the week — that's what goes into the forecast review on Thursday.

mistakes.explanation: 'Rise' is intransitive — it does not take a direct object. 'The deal has risen to negotiate stage' means the deal moved up through the stages on its own. 'Raise' is transitive — someone or something raises something else: 'we raised the deal to negotiate stage', 'the manager raised the probability to 80%'. 'Has raised' without a direct object is non-standard — 'raise' requires something to be raised. The pair: raise (transitive) = to move something upward; rise (intransitive) = to move upward by itself. The same distinction applies to: lay/lie, set/sit, fell/fall. 'The temperature has risen', 'the forecast has risen', 'the deal has risen' — all intransitive, using 'rise', not 'raise'.

'Discuss' is a transitive verb that already means 'talk about' — adding 'about' is redundant and non-standard. 'I'd like to discuss your reengagement plan' is the correct form. 'Discuss about your plan' treats 'discuss' as if it were an intransitive verb like 'talk' ('talk about X'), but 'discuss' takes a direct object directly without a preposition: 'discuss the plan', 'discuss the deal', 'discuss the risk'. This error is extremely common in formal writing — particularly among speakers whose first language uses a preposition in this construction. Other transitive verbs that do not take 'about': 'address', 'consider', 'examine', 'review', 'analyse'.

'Focus on' is a phrasal verb that takes a gerund — the '-ing' form — as its complement. 'Focus on identifying the pattern', 'focus on developing the skill', 'focus on closing the deal'. The preposition 'on' must be followed by a gerund, not by 'to' + infinitive. 'Focus on to identify' mixes the gerund requirement of 'on' with the infinitive marker 'to', producing a non-standard hybrid. This error reflects a confusion between two valid constructions: 'focus on + gerund' (phrasal verb) and 'try/aim/seek + to + infinitive' (infinitive construction). The rule: any preposition — on, in, of, about, for — is followed by a gerund when it takes a verb complement, never by 'to' + infinitive.

finishTheLine.instructions: The sales leader starts a sentence. Work with your partner to finish it naturally using sophisticated sales leadership language.

items.customerLine: Jordan: I think the deal is in good shape — I'm just waiting for Marcus to come back.
items.salespersonStart: Waiting is a strategy — but it's a passive one. Tell me what 'good shape' looks like in observable terms.
items.suggestedCompletion: When was your last meaningful contact with Marcus — not an email he didn't respond to, but a real conversation? What was the explicit next step you agreed at the end of your last call? And how many people inside Meridian have you spoken to in the past three weeks, other than Marcus? Because 'good shape' based on one stakeholder who isn't responding is a different thing from 'good shape' based on a mutual action plan, a named champion, and a CFO conversation already scheduled. Which one do you have?

items.customerLine: Jordan: I know I should call Marcus — I've just been putting it off.
items.salespersonStart: That's the most honest thing you've said in this review — and it's exactly the kind of thing I want you to say out loud, because it tells us both something useful.
items.suggestedCompletion: What's behind the avoidance? Because when experienced reps put off a call they know they should make, it's usually one of three things: they're not sure what to say, they're worried the answer will be bad news, or they're carrying a vague sense that the deal isn't as strong as the pipeline says it is. Which one is closest to the truth — and if it's the last one, I'd rather know that now and adjust the forecast honestly than hold it in commit and find out in week eight.

items.customerLine: Jordan: My commit number is £190,000 — but I feel like I should be able to get to £250,000.
items.salespersonStart: I'll take the £190,000 as your commit — that goes into the leadership forecast and I'll stake my credibility on it. The gap to £250,000 is what I want to turn into a plan.
items.suggestedCompletion: Walk me through the £60,000 between those two numbers. Which specific deals sit in that gap — and for each one, what is the specific action, the specific person, and the specific date that makes them closable in Q3? If you can name those three things for each deal, you have a plan. If you can't, you have an aspiration — which is useful to have, but not something I can commit to upward. Let's build the plan right now.
